goldens.comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:13 stores RSS/Atom contents as unsanitized raw_html, enabling persistent XSS when rendered with raw post.cooked

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real security concern. Looking at the diff: 1) In topic_embed.rb line 21, PostCreator is called with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]` which bypasses normal cooking/sanitization. 2) In post.rb lines 131-133, when cook_method is raw_html, it returns `raw` directly without any sanitization. 3) The contents come from RSS feeds (poll_feed.rb) or remote URLs (import_remote) and are stored/rendered without sanitization. 4) In best.html.erb line 17, `raw post.cooked` outputs the content directly. This creates a persistent XSS vulnerability where malicious content in RSS feeds or embedded URLs would be rendered as raw HTML to users viewing the embedded comments.

adjudication_records.issue_text: app/models/topic_embed.rb:45 follows redirects without revalidating the destination host, allowing an approved host to redirect requests to internal services and enable SSRF

adjudication.rationale: Looking at app/models/topic_embed.rb:45, the code uses `open(url).read` via ruby-readability to fetch remote content. The `open` method from open-uri does follow redirects by default. However, the finding claims an 'approved host' can redirect to internal services. The code at line 45 is in `import_remote` which takes a URL parameter. Looking at how this is called: in topic_retriever.rb's `fetch_http` method, it calls `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, @embed_url)` where `@embed_url` has already been validated in `invalid_host?` to match `SiteSetting.embeddable_host`. The issue is that while the initial URL's host is validated, if that URL returns an HTTP redirect to an internal service (like http://localhost, http://169.254.169.254 for cloud metadata, etc.), the `open()` call will follow that redirect without re-validating the destination. This is a legitimate SSRF vulnerability - an attacker controlling content on the approved embeddable_host could set up a redirect to internal services.

adjudication_records.issue_text: spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:42 expects TopicRetriever to be invoked even though the controller now uses Jobs.enqueue, causing the test to fail and leaving enqueue behavior untested

adjudication.rationale: Looking at the test in spec/controllers/embed_controller_spec.rb:42, it expects TopicRetriever.new to be called and return a mock retriever. However, examining the controller code in app/controllers/embed_controller.rb, when topic_id is nil, it calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` which enqueues a job, not directly calling TopicRetriever. The TopicRetriever is actually called inside the job (lib/jobs/regular/retrieve_topic.rb). So the test is mocking TopicRetriever directly, but the controller doesn't call TopicRetriever directly - it enqueues a job. This means the test expectation `TopicRetriever.expects(:new).returns(retriever)` will fail because TopicRetriever.new is never called directly by the controller. The test is incorrectly structured for how the code actually works.

adjudication_records.issue_text: lib/tasks/disqus.thor:117 removes the --category option and category assignment, breaking Disqus imports that need topics placed in a selected category

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that the --category option and related code were removed from lib/tasks/disqus.thor. Lines 117 (method_option :category) and 141-144 (category_id lookup and usage) were deleted. The PostCreator call was replaced with TopicEmbed.import_remote which doesn't accept a category parameter. This is a real breaking change - users who previously relied on the --category flag to place imported Disqus topics into a specific category will no longer be able to do so. The functionality was removed without replacement.

adjudication_records.issue_text: db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb:3 adds force: true to an existing table-creation migration, which can drop top_topics and cause destructive data loss when migrations are replayed against a partially initialized database

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a change to db/migrate/20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb where 'force: true' is added to create_table. Looking at the diff, this is indeed a modification to an existing migration file (the diff shows it changing from 'create_table :top_topics do |t|' to 'create_table :top_topics, force: true do |t|'). Adding 'force: true' to a migration that may have already run in production is dangerous because if migrations are replayed or run again, it will drop the existing table and recreate it, causing data loss. This is a real correctness/data safety issue - modifying existing migrations with destructive options is a known anti-pattern in Rails.
